title: Samajik Samarasata: Thengadi, Ambedkar and the idea of social harmony
author: Editorial Desk
summary: Thengadi, Ambedkar and the Samajik Samarasata Manch: what the accounts say, and what Ambedkar did as India's labour minister in the 1940s.
body:
Few names appear as often in Indian public life as that of **Dr B. R. Ambedkar**, and few organisation-builders thought as long about him as **Dattopant Thengadi**, the founder of the Bharatiya Mazdoor Sangh (BMS). This post looks at that connection: what the available accounts say about how the two men were linked, what Ambedkar actually did for working people, and why the word *samarasata*, or social harmony, sits so close to the heart of BMS's self-description. Where the evidence comes from organisations that are themselves part of the story, we say so.

## Two lives, briefly

Dattopant Thengadi was born on 10 November 1920 in Arvi, in Maharashtra's Wardha district, and died on 14 October 2004 in Pune. He trained in law, served as a full-time RSS pracharak from 1942, and sat in the Rajya Sabha for two terms between 1964 and 1976. Wikipedia's entry lists a long run of institutions that he founded or helped to found, among them the Bharatiya Mazdoor Sangh in 1955, the Bharatiya Kisan Sangh in 1979, the Swadeshi Jagaran Manch and the Samajik Samarasata Manch.

Bhimrao Ramji Ambedkar, born in 1891, died on 6 December 1956 at his home in Delhi, three days after finishing his last manuscript, *The Buddha and His Dhamma*. He chaired the Drafting Committee of the Constituent Assembly from August 1947 to January 1950, and was independent India's first Law and Justice Minister. Before all that, he was a minister of labour in colonial India, which is the part of his career that matters most to a trade union blog.

## What the accounts say about Thengadi and Ambedkar

The link between the two is described differently in different places, so it is worth being precise. An article in ThePrint by a writer associated with the RSS-affiliated Indraprastha Vishwa Samvad Kendra says that Thengadi was a point of contact between Ambedkar and the RSS from the 1940s, that he served as a secretary of the Scheduled Castes Federation while Ambedkar chaired it, and that he acted as Ambedkar's election agent in the Bhandara by-election. The same article says he wrote about those meetings in a Hindi book titled *Dr Ambedkar aur Samajik Kranti ki Yatra*. The piece notes that its claims are disputed by some readers, so it is best read as the RSS family's own account.

Organiser's tribute to Thengadi, also from within the same family of organisations, says he was profoundly influenced by Ambedkar, alongside Golwalkar and Deendayal Upadhyaya, and that he also worked for Ambedkar and formed an Adim Jati Sangh. It adds that his last book was on Ambedkar and that he completed it in July 2004, a few months before his death. It says he wanted to present Ambedkar in a true light, drawing on his own experience.

We could not confirm every detail independently. The Wikipedia article on Thengadi, for instance, lists Ambedkar among his influences but does not mention a post in the Scheduled Castes Federation. A fair reading is that Thengadi knew Ambedkar's circle, admired him, and spent a good part of his later life promoting Ambedkar's memory within the Sangh family.

## The Samajik Samarasata Manch

Thengadi is listed as a founder of the **Samajik Samarasata Manch**, a forum created to promote social harmony across caste lines. BMS's own account of his life, which an earlier version of this post relied on, dates its formation to **14 April 1983**, Ambedkar Jayanti. Other sources we consulted, including Wikipedia and an obituary on the Thengadi archive site, list the Manch among his organisations without giving a date, so the choice of that particular day should be read as BMS's account. Whatever the exact date, the intention is clear: to place the memory of Ambedkar, and the fight against untouchability, inside a movement that is often seen mainly through its economic and labour work.

## Ambedkar as a labour leader

Ambedkar's labour record is well documented, and it is the strongest reason this subject belongs on a union blog.

- In **August 1936** he founded the Independent Labour Party. According to a BMS page on Ambedkar, the party won 14 of the 17 seats it contested in the 1937 provincial elections in Bombay, and it spoke for tenants, peasants and the unorganised poor as well as factory workers.
- In 1938 he opposed the Industrial Disputes Bill, which in his view amounted to a suspension of workers' civil liberties. He argued that the right to strike was part of the right to freedom.
- From **July 1942** until 1946 he served as the Labour Member of the Viceroy's Executive Council, in effect the country's labour minister.
- On **27 November 1942**, at the seventh session of the Indian Labour Conference in New Delhi, he announced a reduction of the working day to eight hours. Accounts differ on the figure it replaced, with some saying fourteen hours and others ten, so we simply say that the eight-hour day was announced there.
- He promoted tripartite conferences in which government, employers and workers sat at the same table, and he supported legislation that would have made employers recognise trade unions.
- On **9 December 1943** he went down to the collieries of Dhanbad to see conditions himself, examining women's amenities and miners' housing. He also visited mica mines in Koderma. Soon afterwards the ban on women working underground in coal mines was lifted, a decision that has been debated ever since.
- Laws on maternity benefit, factories and welfare funds are among those associated with his tenure, though the sources differ on which particular statute should be credited to which year.

None of this was a distant matter of high politics. A worker in a Dhanbad colliery in the 1940s, or a mica-splitter in Koderma, lived the questions that a minister was then trying to answer: how many hours, what safety, what housing, and who speaks for the worker.

## Why caste and labour cannot be separated

The Indian working class has never been an abstract category. In factories, on construction sites, in mines and in municipal services, jobs have been distributed by caste as often as by skill, and dignity at work has depended on who a person was born to. That is why Ambedkar's life makes sense as a labour story: the Independent Labour Party, the Labour Member's office, and the Constitution's guarantees against untouchability belonged to one argument. A union that wishes to speak for all workers has to deal with that history honestly, and not only with wage tables.

## BMS and the idea of samarasata

BMS describes its membership as drawn from every region and community, and its leadership has included people from many backgrounds. Its President, Hiranmay Pandya, has said that BMS is not only about pay, perks and promotion, and that social harmony is among the themes it has long worked on, together with the environment and swadeshi. Translating such statements into daily union practice is slower work. It means asking, in each union and each workplace, who gets promoted, who gets the cleaner tasks, who is invited to speak, and whether the answers look like the membership.

*Samarasata* is a word that implies more than tolerance. It suggests a society in which every person is treated with equal respect, in the same spirit in which a river is made up of many streams. For a trade union, it is a worthy word to keep close, and Ambedkar's example, as a legislator who walked into a mine and asked about housing, is a demanding standard to measure oneself against.
